analysis.title: The Flow Show: A Tail of Two Cities
key_insights: Year-to-date returns as of 9/30/2026: oil +61.8%, global stocks +12.1%, US stocks +12.0%, US dollar +3.8%, cash +2.7%, HY bonds -0.3%, IG -3.2%, bitcoin -3.4%, gold -3.8%, government bonds -4.1%.
Q3 winners were bitcoin +43%, oil +42%, software +18% and Mag7 +11%. Losers were zero-coupon bonds -15%, semis -11%, industrials -10% and Korea -8%.

Tighter financial conditions are hurting equity breadth: 400 S&P 500 stocks trade below their 50-day moving average and 300 below their 200-day, while the market trades 'long artificial intelligence' (NDX) and 'short artificial irrelevance' (SPW). BofA says the 1999 analog remains intact.

BofA's view is that the market is risk-off until the US dollar peaks. The dollar is rising on credit event risk, visible in the Australian dollar, French bonds, risk parity (RPAR), bond insurers (AGO) and tech CDS (ORCL), which BofA reads as deleveraging price action.

BofA expects a policy panic (open-ended Treasury buybacks, yield curve control) to limit the downside, because yields cannot be allowed to hit the AI capex boom and stocks going into the midterms. The exception is small/mid-caps (MDY below $666, IJR below $135) following the banks' breakdown. 'Peak growth optimism' is negative for tech.

Bull case for AI is 'it's the railroads this time'. Peak sector concentration was 40% for internet, Japan, the Nifty Fifty and the roaring 20s, but 63% for railroads in 1881. AI capex of 3.5-4% of GDP compares with a 5% railroad peak, and semiconductor prices are rising while freight rates were deflating at the railroad top.

Bear case for AI: railroad booms were backstopped by falling Treasury yields, which is not the case today. Railroad tops in 1973 and 1981 coincided with credit events, sharp declines in liquidity and capital outflows driven by geopolitical events.
Weekly flows: $18.8bn to bonds, $15.8bn to stocks, $0.9bn to crypto, $0.7bn to gold, and $118.0bn out of cash on quarter-end.

Investors are starting to buy bonds and bond-sensitive sectors. Long-term bonds took in $7.4bn (largest since May 2025), municipal bonds $4.2bn (largest ever, data since 2004), Europe equities $1.3bn (largest since Feb 2026), China equities $3.7bn (largest in 9 weeks), tech $3.3bn (largest in 5 weeks) and utilities $1.0bn (largest since Dec 2025).

BofA private clients hold $4.6tn AUM: 66.3% stocks (record high), 17.1% bonds, 9.4% cash (record low). Mag7 is 16% of AUM, Treasuries 4%, international stocks 4%, gold 0.3%. Over four weeks they bought bank loan, muni and TIPS ETFs and sold utilities, tech and financials ETFs.

The BofA Bull & Bear Indicator fell to 8.8 from 9.3 on wider risky-bond spreads, HY bond outflows and deteriorating global index breadth (net 27% of global equity indices below both 50d and 200dma, worst since Mar 2026). The signal is Sell. The 'old' indicator is at 6.2.

On bonds, BofA says a credit event or recession is needed for a 100-200bps fall in yields. Because allocators are very long stocks and very short bonds, BofA says 'buy humiliation' and start adding bonds. Long-run Treasury returns are the worst in 100 years, and bond portfolios are nearing equity-like returns.

US IG tech bonds (CITE) are down 9% over the past year, with yield up from 4.5% to 6.2%. Hyperscaler long-term yields are Oracle 8.4%, Meta 7.5% and Google 6.9%. BofA argues the AI buildout is backstopped by the US government, so these yields may soon attract buyers.

Railroad history: the first bubble ended in 1873 on excess capex and a credit crunch (stocks up 3x over 1861-72, capex peaked near 5% of GDP, Jay Cooke & Company collapsed, about 115 railroads went bankrupt). The second ended in 1881 on excess capacity and freight-rate deflation (stocks up 2.5x, 63% of the US market, construction down 42% in 1882, a 1882-85 recession).
AI hyperscaler capex of $1.2-1.4tn is on course to reach 3.5-4% of GDP in 2027. The computers and peripheral equipment proxy rose from $145bn (Q3'23) to $401bn (Q2'26).

Fixed income flows: IG inflows for 2 weeks ($3.5bn), HY outflows resumed ($1.4bn), EM debt inflows for 9 weeks ($2.3bn), munis inflows for 24 weeks ($4.2bn), Treasuries inflows for 14 weeks ($10.8bn), TIPS inflows for 35 weeks ($0.5bn), bank loan inflows for 4 weeks ($1.1bn).

Equity flows: US outflows for 2 weeks ($2.7bn), Japan inflows for 6 weeks ($1.8bn), Europe inflows resumed ($1.3bn), EM inflows resumed ($3.2bn). By style, US growth saw outflows of $4.5bn and US large cap $3.9bn, while US small cap took in $0.3bn.

2026 YTD ranked returns (USD, to 9/30): Korea equities +98.3%, Taiwan +70.7%, ACWI Info Tech +34.8%, ACWI Energy +30.6%, EM equities +23.7%, Japan +23.0%, US equities +12.6%, gold -4.3%, bitcoin -4.6%, India equities -14.7%, China equities -11.7%.
Overbought/oversold vs 200-day average: Taiwan equities +22.5%, Korea +19.4%, ACWI Info Tech +17.3%, Brent +17.5%, gold -8.5%, silver -17.1%, 30-year Treasury -7.3%.

tension_points.bull_case: AI capex at 3.5-4% of GDP is below the 5% railroad peak, and semiconductor prices are rising while freight rates were deflating at the railroad top. The AI buildout is also backstopped by the US government.
tension_points.bear_case: Railroad booms were backstopped by falling Treasury yields, which is not the case today. Railroad tops in 1873, 1881, 1973 and 1981 were tied to credit events, liquidity declines and capital outflows, and the hyperscaler bond yields at 6.9-8.4% show rising funding costs.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A credit event or liquidity shock, or small/mid-caps breaking MDY below $666 and IJR below $135.

tension_points.bull_case: Long-run Treasury returns are the worst in 100 years, allocators are very short bonds, and IG tech and hyperscaler bond yields now approach equity-like returns.
tension_points.bear_case: Only a credit event or recession would bring a 100-200bps decline in yields, and a final melt-up in Treasury yields is possible.
